definition: A way of storing energy, such as kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, chemical, thermal, nuclear, electrostatic or magnetic.
The energy an object has due to its motion. Depends on both mass and speed.
The energy stored in an object due to its height above the ground. Increases as an object is lifted higher.
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed object, such as a spring or elastic band.
Energy stored in the bonds of chemical substances, such as food, fuel or batteries.
Energy stored in an object due to the motion of its particles — also called internal energy.
The movement of energy from one store to another, by heating, by mechanical work, by electrical work or by radiation.
The energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance. Measured in joules (J). W = Fs.
The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done. Measured in watts (W). P = E/t or P = W/t.
The unit of power. 1 watt = 1 joule per second.
The unit of energy and work done.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred from one store to another. The total energy always remains the same.
The proportion of energy input that is usefully transferred. Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (can be expressed as a decimal or percentage).
Energy that is transferred to a useful store — the energy that does what you want it to do.
Energy that is transferred to an unwanted store, usually as heat or sound.
The spreading out of energy into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, making it less useful.
Reducing friction between moving parts using oil or grease, which reduces wasted energy as heat.
The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Measured in J/kg°C.
A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Measured in degrees Celsius (°C) or Kelvin (K).
Materials or methods that reduce the rate of heat transfer, keeping objects warm or cool for longer.
An energy resource that is naturally replenished and will not run out, such as wind, solar, tidal or hydroelectric power.
An energy resource that will eventually run out and cannot be replenished in a short time, such as coal, oil, gas and nuclear fuel.
Coal, oil and natural gas — formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms. Non-renewable energy resources.
Energy harnessed from sunlight using solar cells (photovoltaic) or solar thermal panels.
Energy generated by wind turbines, which use the kinetic energy of wind to generate electricity.
Electricity generated by using the gravitational potential energy of water stored at height, released through turbines.
Electricity generated by harnessing the kinetic energy of tidal water movements.
A non-renewable energy resource (e.g. uranium) used in nuclear power stations to generate electricity through nuclear fission.
The total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an individual, event, organisation or product, expressed in CO₂ equivalent.
The network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to homes and businesses across the country.
